title-group.article-title: Inpatient outcomes associated with atrial fibrillation among adults hospitalized with lung cancer.

contrib-group.aff: Eastgate Cancer Research Network, New York, NY
Southern Clinical Oncology Center, Atlanta, GA
Pacific Precision Medicine Institute, San Francisco, CA

permissions.copyright-statement: © 2026 by American Society of Clinical Oncology

abstract.p: Background: Patients hospitalized with lung cancer frequently have complex medical comorbidities, but the clinical impact of concurrent atrial fibrillation is not well defined. We examined inpatient outcomes and resource utilization associated with this complication. Methods: We analyzed the National Inpatient Sample for 2018–2022. Adult hospitalizations with a diagnosis of lung cancer were identified using ICD-10-CM codes and stratified by the presence or absence of atrial fibrillation. Weighted national estimates were generated. Multivariable logistic and linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, race, payer, hospital characteristics, metastatic disease, and comorbidity burden. Results: Among an estimated 236,415 hospitalizations for lung cancer, 29,172 included atrial fibrillation. Patients with the complication had a median age of 71 years, and 48.6% were female. Mean length of stay was 7.0 versus 5.2 days, and mean hospital charges were $90,340 versus $68,110. After adjustment, atrial fibrillation was associated with higher odds of ischemic stroke (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.6), acute respiratory failure (aOR 1.8), and in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.5). Conclusions: Concurrent atrial fibrillation identifies a clinically vulnerable subgroup of hospitalized patients with lung cancer and is associated with greater morbidity, mortality, and resource use. Early recognition and coordinated oncologic and medical management may improve inpatient care. Research Sponsor: None.
